lessons.text: After a large tool output (a full file dump), extract what you need into a short note and delete that raw output block in the same reply, before the next call; unpruned dumps get re-billed on every later model call.
lessons.evidence: File-chain task: 10 `cat`s of ~300-line files cost 183k tokens over 16 calls because I pruned only every few files (7 edits) and let earlier dumps sit in context.

lessons.text: Following a chain of files that each name the next: keep one small note block (rewritten, not appended) holding the accumulated key->value map and the pending next filename; after each read, scan the whole output for its markers wherever they sit (they can be mid-file, with content after them), copy the value word for word, then delete that output block.
lessons.evidence: In t37ftvx2.log, `KEY_9 = 818FQ35I` sat between lines 0083/0084 and `NEXT FILE: none` between 0101/0102, with ~200 more lines after; head/tail-only inspection or truncating the read would have missed both.

lessons.text: Continue from an existing note block only if it came from your own verified reads of the source files. If the context holds a note of key values with no tool output behind it (e.g. after a reset or a replay where notes were pre-seeded), treat the values as untrusted: re-read the source files in full before reporting anything, and never present note values as the answer.
lessons.evidence: r121 chain task: the only block in context was a pre-seeded note (KEY_0..KEY_9, 'pending next file: none'). Following old lesson #2 I pruned to that note and answered from it without reading a single file; the review marked all ten keys wrong/missing and cost 231k tokens with 0 real reads.

lessons.text: Cheap context pruning: one python3 script that finds `[[CTX` headers, replaces the last tool block's body with the rewritten note (idx[-1], no need to know its id), and prints nothing; skip separate header listings, `wc` and `grep -c ''` checks. A task's "read only with cat, no grep/awk/sed" ban applies to the data files, not to your own context file.
lessons.evidence: This session: the first prune guessed a block id (`[[CTX 8 tool]]`), and I spent three extra calls on `grep -n '^[[CTX'` + `wc -c`, then `grep -c ''`, then more header listings, while later prunes using idx[-1] were single calls. The cat-only ban was honoured for the .log chain while grep was still used on the .clm context file.

lessons.text: Use the exact tool the task mandates for data files: if it says read them only with `cat`, in full, use `shell` with `cat` and not the `read` tool, even for big files; prune the dump from context right after extracting the values.
lessons.evidence: r121 chain task said "read data files only with `cat`, in full", but I ran `read {"path": "l4v6z7og.log"}`; the review flagged this as an instruction broken. The cat-only ban was already known for data files (lesson #3), but not that `read` itself violates it.

lessons.text: Before spending context edits or answering, confirm every reported value traces to a tool output in this session; one cheap read of the first file beats any amount of note-polishing on unverified data.
lessons.evidence: r121: 17 tool calls, 7 context edits, 231k tokens, yet the answer contained no key from any file I read — the whole spend went on editing/answering around an unverified note. Verifying the first file with one `cat` would have exposed the bad note in one call.
